newsitem.title: INDIA: Political woes may set back Indian economic recovery.
newsitem.headline: Political woes may set back Indian economic recovery.

text.p: The one bright spot in India's political chaos is a collective will to pass Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's widely acclaimed budget, analysts said.
It diverts, at least for now, some attention away from a potential power vacuum, a slowing economic recovery and battered business confidence.
"I think the Indian economy is in the process of getting depoliticised," Sanjeev Mohta, head of research at brokerage James Capel B & K, told Reuters.

Bitter recriminations followed the defeat of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 10-month old minority coalition in a confidence vote on Friday, but all sides appeared to realise endangering the unpassed budget would rebound badly on them.
Cross-party goodwill toward the tax cutting and pro-growth budget will be put to the test in a specially convened three-day debate on the bill starting April 21.
"It looks like the budget will go through. It is a good sign -- economic issues are separated from political issues," Ravi Kumar, chief foreign exchange dealer at ABN AMRO Bank NV in Bombay, said.

The economy can do without another political handicap. The latest data shows growth in industrial output slowed to 8.3 percent in the nine months through December 1996 from 11.4 percent for the same year-ago period.

Equity markets are already factoring into prices a smooth passage for the Finance Bill. And analysts are leaving largely untouched corporate earning forecasts based on Chidambaram's generous measures.

Share trading on Saturday, compared with recent wild movements, was relatively sober the day despite the government's fall. The Bombay Stock Exchange top-30 index dropped 44.01 points, or 1.21 percent, to 3,589.72.
The BSE index hit 4,007.91 on March 3 in the euphoria a few days after Chidambaram presented his budget gameplan.
"There had been strong hopes that the budget will boost demand, in turn leading to a pick-up in economic activity. This is now going to be delayed," Mohta said.
That will hurt tax inflows, undermining Chidambaram's supply-side economic strategy, which banked on the tax cuts generating more wealth and broadening the tax base.

The budget wrote in a 17.1 percent increase in tax revenue to raise 1,531 billion rupees in 1997/98. Any shortfall will hit a planned reduction in the fiscal deficit to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product from last year's five percent target.
Mohta was optimistic a new government coalition could be pulled together within days but said it could take as long as three months.
If Chidambaram stayed at the helm of the economy all the better because his strategy needed to be followed for a number of years to work, analysts agreed.
A new government also needs to take charge soon for the sake of the privatisation programme, they said.
"Divestments will not take place without a government. I think there'll also be some holding back of foreign investments until the political situation crystallises," Mohta said.

Chidamabaram's budget had banked on sales of partial stakes in state-owned firms raising 48 billion rupees ($1.3 billion) in 1997/98 (April-March). Last year, the target was 50 billion rupees, but sickly market conditions stalled launches and kept the actual figure closer to five billion.
And commitments of direct foreign investment, needed to elevate India to the ranks of the Asian Tigers, will be withheld as long as there is a question over who runs the country.

India wants $10 billion of foreign direct investment (FDI) annually for the next few years to remove the bottlenecks caused by creaking infrastructure, but actual inflows of FDI in the nine months through December 1996 totalled just $1.71 billion.

A leadership vacuum resulting from either the formation of a weak coalition, or a second general election inside a year, will paralyse the decision-making in New Delhi needed to keep India's economy on an upward track, analysts said.

Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) were expected to sink more money into India's equity and capital markets in response to the budget's reaffirmation of India's comittment to reform. But now they can afford to wait and pick their levels while the politics settle down. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
